idiom_name: std::condition_variable predicate loop on a std::chrono::steady_clock deadline (or Boost.Asio steady_timer)
implementation_notes: The standard library provides the timing substrate but no scheduling or health framework, so the watchman structure - per-subject expectation, last-seen stamp, evaluation, escalation - is written by hand: the arrival path stores a monotonic deadline (steady_clock::now() + period) under a mutex and notifies, and the monitor evaluates wait_for with a predicate rather than trusting the return value, because spurious wake-ups are allowed. C++20 adds std::jthread with a stop_token so the monitor loop can be cancelled and joined deterministically, and Boost.Asio's steady_timer is the library alternative when an io_context already drives the process. std::system_clock is never the right clock here.
pitfalls: std::system_clock steps with NTP and manual clock changes, producing phantom silences and alarms that never fire; every deadline and stamp must come from std::chrono::steady_clock.
wait_for may wake spuriously and its return value alone does not mean the timeout elapsed - always re-check the predicate (the predicate overload or an explicit loop).

std::atomic<std::chrono::steady_clock::time_point> is not a supported or lock-free specialization on common ABIs; if the stamp must be shared without a mutex, store steady_clock ticks in std::atomic<long long> and derive silence from that.
Alert dispatch inside the monitor (paging, DNS, SMTP, logging to a blocking sink) stalls the loop that is supposed to notice the next silence; hand the alarm to a worker or queue.

Shutdown must not race a producer that is still stamping: stop the arrival path (or drive the close with a stop_token) before joining the monitor, or the last wait_for can hold shutdown for a full silence budget.

variants.name: C++20 jthread with stop_token cancellation
variants.implementation_notes: The C++20 realization makes the monitor a self-joining component: std::jthread owns the loop and requests_stop() ends it without a bespoke shutdown flag, while condition_variable_any::wait_for(lock, stop_token, deadline) wakes on cancellation as well as on the deadline. The last-seen stamp is an atomic tick count so arrival paths never block behind the monitor.
pitfalls: stop_token-aware waits must still re-check the predicate, and a stop request that arrives between predicate check and wait is only reliable through the token overload.
The atomic tick counter must be monotonic ticks, not seconds since epoch, or it silently reintroduces the wall-clock dependency.

variants.name: Boost.Asio steady_timer deadline in an io_context
variants.idiom_name: boost::asio::steady_timer + expires_after, re-armed by the arrival handler
variants.implementation_notes: Where an Asio io_context already runs, the watchman is a timer instead of a thread: the arrival handler calls expires_after(period) (and async_wait again), and the wait handler is the absence alarm; the completion handler model matches the rest of the process and keeps the monitor single-threaded. Asio's steady_timer is monotonic, so the deadline survives clock changes.
pitfalls: expires_after() on a timer with a pending async_wait cancels that wait with operation_aborted: the handler must distinguish genuine expiry from cancellation, or every arrival pages.
A single-threaded io_context must not run blocking alert I/O inside the wait handler - it stops all timers on that context while reporting.
